original_value: AbstractExotic behaviour of mechanical metamaterials often relies on an internal transformation of the underlying microstructure triggered by its local instabilities, rearrangements, and rotations. Depending on the presence and magnitude of such a transformation, effective properties of a metamaterial may change significantly. To capture this phenomenon accurately and efficiently, homogenization schemes are required that reflect microstructural as well as macro-structural instabilities, large deformations, and non-local effects. To this end, a micromorphic computational homogenization scheme has recently been developed, which employs the particular microstructural transformation as a non-local mechanism, magnitude of which is governed by an additional coupled partial differential equation. Upon discretizing the resulting problem it turns out that the macroscopic stiffness matrix requires integration of macro-element basis functions as well as their derivatives, thus calling for higher-order integration rules. Because evaluation of a constitutive law in multiscale schemes involves an expensive solution of a non-linear boundary value problem, computational efficiency of the micromorphic scheme can be improved by reducing the number of integration points. Therefore, the goal of this paper is to investigate reduced-order schemes in computational homogenization, with emphasis on the stability of the resulting elements. In particular, arguments for lowering the order of integration from expensive mass-matrix to a cheaper stiffness-matrix equivalent are outlined first. An efficient one-point integration quadrilateral element is then introduced and a proper hourglass stabilization is discussed. Performance of the resulting set of elements is finally tested on a benchmark bending example, showing that we achieve accuracy comparable to the full quadrature rules, whereas computational cost decreases proportionally to the reduction in the number of quadrature points used.

result.paraphrase: AbstractExotic behavior in mechanical metamaterials often stems from internal microstructural transformations induced by local instabilities, rearrangements, and rotations. The effective properties of a metamaterial can change markedly depending on whether such a transformation occurs and how large it is. Accurate and efficient treatment of this phenomenon requires homogenization methods that account for microstructural and macrostructural instabilities, large deformations, and non-local effects. A micromorphic computational homogenization scheme has recently been proposed for this purpose, using the specific microstructural transformation as a non-local mechanism whose magnitude is controlled by an additional coupled partial differential equation. After discretization, the macroscopic stiffness matrix must be integrated with macro-element basis functions and their derivatives, which necessitates higher-order integration rules. Since evaluating a constitutive law in multiscale schemes requires solving an expensive nonlinear boundary value problem, the computational efficiency of the micromorphic scheme can be improved by reducing the number of integration points. The aim of this paper is therefore to examine reduced-order schemes in computational homogenization, with particular attention to element stability. First, arguments are given for reducing the integration order from an expensive mass-matrix equivalent to a cheaper stiffness-matrix equivalent. Next, an efficient one-point integration quadrilateral element is introduced and appropriate hourglass stabilization is discussed. Finally, the performance of the resulting elements is evaluated on a benchmark bending example, demonstrating accuracy comparable to full quadrature rules while computational cost drops in proportion to the reduction in quadrature points.
